title: The Wired Side of the Wireless Network
lead: How APs and the controller get connected — access or trunk, LAG on the WLC, controller ports and interfaces, and management vs. dynamic interfaces.

sections.title: How an access point gets connected

blocks.text: The rule is simple, and it's a favorite exam question:

items: **Local mode (a regular AP on CAPWAP)** — the switch port is configured as **access** in the VLAN where the APs themselves live. All client traffic rides inside the CAPWAP tunnel, so no client VLANs are needed on this port.
**FlexConnect with local switching** or an **autonomous AP** — the port is configured as a **trunk**: client VLANs exit to the network right here.

blocks.text: Plus power: an AP needs **PoE** (802.3af for simple ones, 802.3at/bt for 802.11ac/ax) or an external injector. The power negotiation mode is **auto** (the switch detects the device itself and then guarantees it the rated power) — the same auto/static principle covered in the chapter on physical network components. For new Wi-Fi 6/6E APs with two or three radios and aggregate throughput above a gigabit, you use not regular Gigabit Ethernet but **Multigigabit** (802.3bz) — category 5e/6 cabling carries 2.5 or 5 Gbps without rewiring, only over a shorter distance than the formal standard for that category.

! Port to a lightweight AP in local mode
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/10
 description AP-2F-01
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 60          ! AP VLAN
 spanning-tree portfast
 spanning-tree bpduguard enable

blocks.title: Trap
paras: "AP in local mode → trunk" is the most common wrong answer. A trunk is needed where client frames exit to the wired network at the AP itself — in local mode, they exit at the controller instead.

blocks.text: On a WLC, "port" and "interface" are separate concepts.

head: Port
Purpose
rows: the main physical port to the network; carries CAPWAP and client traffic; usually a **trunk**
a separate out-of-band management port, its own subnet, no routing
link to a backup controller (HA SSO)

blocks.text: The switch port the WLC plugs into is a **trunk**, because the controller hands off traffic from different WLANs to different VLANs.

**LAG** on a WLC bundles physical ports into one logical port (the equivalent of EtherChannel). On the switch side this is an EtherChannel in mode **`on`** — the controller doesn't take part in LACP, and that's a separate exam fact worth remembering. Enabling LAG requires a controller reboot, and all interfaces are automatically bound to the logical group. The recommended load-balancing mode on the switch itself is **src-dst-ip** (`port-channel load-balance src-dst-ip`): for some WLC platforms (the older 4400, WiSM1, 3750G, WiSM2) this isn't just a recommendation but a hard requirement — otherwise fragmented CAPWAP packets can end up on different physical links and fail to reassemble.

head: Interface
What it is
rows: the address APs use to build CAPWAP tunnels, and the one admins use to reach the GUI
a non-existent address (classically 192.0.2.1) used for DHCP relay, web authentication, and mobility
an interface bound to a client-network VLAN; a WLAN maps onto it
the service port's address, on its own subnet
handled CAPWAP tunnels on older platforms; merged into management on current ones

blocks.text: The chain: **WLAN (SSID) → dynamic interface → VLAN**. That's exactly how wireless traffic lands on the right wired subnet, and it's exactly what's missing when "the client connects but gets no address."

sections.title: What has to line up for it to all work

items: The AP gets an address (typically DHCP in the AP VLAN) and finds the controller — via static configuration, DHCP option 43, or DNS.
**UDP 5246/5247** passes between the AP and the controller — if there's a firewall between them, these ports need to be open.
The switch the WLC plugs into allows the VLANs of every client network (trunk).
A dynamic interface exists on the controller in the right VLAN, with an address and a DHCP server.
The WLAN is mapped to that interface and enabled.

blocks.text: Diagnosing "client can't reach the network" follows this same ladder, bottom to top: is there an association → did authentication succeed → was an address assigned → does the gateway work.

SW1# show cdp neighbors
Device ID    Local Intrfce   Holdtme  Capability   Platform    Port ID
AP-2F-01     Gig 1/0/10      156         T         AIR-AP2802  Gig 0

SW1# show power inline gigabitethernet1/0/10
Interface Admin  Oper       Power   Device              Class Max
Gi1/0/10  auto   on         30.0    AIR-AP2802I-E-K9    4     30.0

SW1# show interfaces trunk        ! on the port to the controller
Port        Vlans allowed and active in management domain
Gi1/0/48    60,70,80
Three things this confirms: the AP is actually connected and recognized, it's getting power, and the client VLANs reach the controller.

sections.title: Diagnostics: the AP gets power but never comes up

blocks.text: **Symptom.** The AP's LED blinks suspiciously long, `show cdp neighbors` on the switch doesn't see the AP at all, even though it's definitely the right cable.
**What we check.** Whether the PoE budget is actually enough for this specific AP, not just whether power is flowing at all:

SW1# show power inline gigabitethernet1/0/10
Interface Admin  Oper       Power   Device   Class Max
Gi1/0/10  auto   off        0.0     n/a      n/a   15.4

**What we found.** `Oper: off` with `Admin: auto` means the switch never completed power negotiation at all: `Max 15.4` shows the port can only deliver 802.3af, while an 802.11ac/ax-family AP needs 802.3at (30 W) for its radios to start normally — the same class distinction covered in the PoE chapter. The AP either doesn't start at all, or comes up in a crippled state (missing one of its radios). The fix isn't a new cable — it's matching the AP's power class against what the specific port can actually deliver, and if needed, moving it to a port that supports 802.3at/bt or adding an injector.

sections.title: Diagnostics: the LAG on the controller won't form

blocks.text: **Symptom.** LAG is enabled on the WLC, and the network-side switch has EtherChannel configured in `active` mode (LACP) — each individual port physically comes up, but no combined channel forms.

**What we found.** The controller **doesn't take part in LACP or PAgP at all** — LAG on a WLC requires mode `on` on the switch side: static bundling with no negotiation. A configured `active`/`desirable` mode waits for negotiation frames the WLC will never send, and the ports stay as separate interfaces instead of one channel — the same outcome as the classic EtherChannel mode mismatch (`active` ↔ `passive` works, `auto` ↔ `auto` doesn't), except here the correct answer is `on`, not protocol negotiation at all.

items: "How should the switch port connected to a lightweight AP in local mode be configured?" — access, in the AP VLAN.
"Which interface on the WLC is used by APs to build CAPWAP tunnels?" — management (on older platforms, AP-manager).
"What is the purpose of the virtual interface?" — web authentication, DHCP relay, mobility; the address isn't routed.
"Which EtherChannel mode is required for a WLC LAG?" — `on`; the controller doesn't negotiate LACP/PAgP.
"A wireless client associates but gets no IP" — check the dynamic interface, the VLAN on the trunk, and DHCP.
"Which port provides out-of-band management?" — service port.

"An AP configured for 802.11ac fails to fully start on a port whose max power shows 15.4 W. What is the issue?" — the port only delivers 802.3af, while the AP needs 802.3at/bt — a PoE class shortfall, not a cabling problem.
"A LAG is configured on the WLC, but the corresponding switch ports use LACP active mode. What is wrong?" — the WLC doesn't take part in LACP/PAgP; the switch side needs static mode `on` for a LAG.

items.q: An AP is running in local mode. What switch port mode does it need?
items.a: Access, in the AP VLAN: no client VLANs appear on this port, and traffic rides inside CAPWAP.

items.q: Which WLC interface maps an SSID onto a wired VLAN?
What EtherChannel mode is used to bundle the link to a controller, and why?
items.a: Mode on: the WLC doesn't take part in LACP or PAgP.

items.q: Why does the controller need a virtual interface with a non-existent address?
items.a: For web authentication, DHCP relay, and mobility support — this address is never routed onto the network.

items.q: An AP isn't joining the controller. What are the first three checks?
items.a: Whether the AP got an IP address; whether it knows the controller's address (static, option 43, DNS); whether UDP 5246/5247 pass between them.

items.q: Show power inline shows Oper: off and Max 15.4 on the port to an 802.11ac AP. What's the problem?
items.a: The port can only deliver 802.3af (15.4 W), while the AP needs 802.3at/bt (30 W or more) for a full start — the AP isn't getting enough power, not losing its cable connection.

items.q: LAG is configured on the WLC, and the switch has EtherChannel in active mode. Will the channel form?
items.a: No: the WLC doesn't take part in LACP; a LAG requires static mode on on the switch side.
